description: The Ships stack: the ships-go game server and the ships-npc simulation that flies every NPC. ships-npc has no metrics endpoint of its own - it pushes its CPU and memory to ships-go over the websocket they already share, and ships-go re-exports them as ships_npc_*, so everything here comes from the single ships-go scrape.

panels.description: 1 when ships-npc is connected to ships-go and reporting. It drops to 0 the moment the controller disconnects, or after 30s of silence if it stops reporting without closing the socket. When this is Down the other ships_npc_* series stop existing rather than freezing at their last value, so gaps in the panels below are expected.
panels.title: NPC simulator

panels.description: Players currently connected to the game.
panels.title: Players online

panels.description: Ships and black holes being flown by ships-npc right now.
panels.title: NPCs simulated

panels.description: As reported by ships-npc itself, as a percentage of ONE core: 100% is one core saturated and a multi-core process can exceed it.
panels.title: ships-npc CPU

panels.description: Average time one simulation tick took, including the update sent to ships-go. Thresholds assume the default 100ms tick; adjust them if you change NPC_TICK_INTERVAL_MS.
panels.title: Avg tick

panels.description: How much of the tick interval the simulation actually consumes. This is THE number for capacity: at 100% a tick no longer fits in its slot and the simulation starts falling behind, whatever the CPU percentage says.
panels.title: Tick budget used

panels.description: Percentage of one core, derived from each process's CPU counter. Both series are rate()d over the scrape window, which is steadier than the instantaneous ships_npc_cpu_percent shown above and survives a restart of either process.
panels.title: CPU

panels.description: Real memory each process holds, as the OS sees it - the figure a container memory limit kills on. Compare with the heap panel below to tell a genuine leak from the Go runtime holding on to freed pages.
panels.title: Resident memory

panels.description: The simulation has one tick interval to do all its work in. When the average tick approaches the budget line, ships-npc is at capacity: it will start missing ticks and NPCs will move in visible jumps.
panels.title: Tick duration vs budget

panels.description: What the simulation is actually being asked to do. Read the CPU and tick panels against this: a rise in either is only interesting relative to the number of entities causing it.
panels.title: Fleet and players
Capacity - how many ships can it fly?

panels.description:
CPU percentage divided by the number of NPCs alive. This is the number to extrapolate from: multiply it by a target fleet size to predict the load before you actually run it. A flat line means the simulation scales linearly; a rising one means something in it is quadratic - which ship-vs-ship collision and targeting naturally are.

The "> 0" filter on the divisor drops the series entirely while no NPCs are alive, so an empty fleet shows a gap rather than reporting the whole process CPU as the cost of nothing.
panels.title: CPU cost per NPC

panels.description: The same idea against the tick budget rather than the CPU: how much of a tick each NPC costs. Divide the tick interval by this to get a rough ceiling on fleet size.
panels.title: Tick time per NPC

panels.description: Live heap objects against heap reserved from the OS, for both services. Live climbing steadily between collections is normal; live climbing ACROSS collections is a leak. Reserved is what shows up in resident memory.
panels.title: Heap in use

panels.description: ships-go runs a goroutine per connection, so this tracks players. ships-npc should sit at a small constant (tick loop, socket reader, metrics reporter) whatever the fleet size - a climbing line there is a goroutine leak, since NPCs are simulated in one loop, not one each.
panels.title: Goroutines

panels.description: Only ships-go is covered here: the Go collector describes the process serving /metrics, and ships-npc reports its numbers by hand rather than shipping a full GC histogram. A long pause in ships-go is a stutter for every connected player, since the broadcast loop stops with it.
panels.title: GC pause time

panels.description: ships-go's sockets and traffic. Open descriptors that climb and never fall are connections that were never closed. Throughput is in bytes per second on the right axis.
panels.title: File descriptors and network

list.description: NPC_TICK_INTERVAL_MS, the time ships-npc has to complete one simulation tick. Used to work out how much of its budget the simulation is consuming.
list.label: Tick budget (ms)
